extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners, patent practitioners, and applicants' attorneys
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on when and how AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) exceptions (including common-ownership and inventor-originated disclosures) apply and on the use and required content of affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.130 to overcome prior art rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(B) exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The exception in AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(B) applies only to subject matter in an intervening U.S. patent document that was publicly disclosed by the inventor or a joint inventor (or another who obtained the subject matter directly or indirectly from the inventor or joint inventor) before the date the subject matter relied upon was effectively filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exception does not necessarily remove the entire disclosure from being prior art; portions of an intervening reference not previously publicly disclosed by the inventor (e.g., D in a reference disclosing A,B,C,D when the inventor disclosed A,B,C) remain prior art under 102(a)(2). If the intervening document is a more general description (e.g., genus) of inventor-disclosed subject matter (e.g., species), the exception can apply to that subject matter in the intervening document. Conversely, a species disclosed later in an intervening document when only a genus was previously disclosed by the inventor remains prior art. If an intervening document discloses an alternative species not previously disclosed by the inventor, that alternative species is prior art because the "subject matter disclosed" requirement is not met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiry for applying 102(b)(2)(B) does not compare claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A determination of whether the 102(b)(2)(B) exception applies does not involve comparing the subject matter of the claimed invention to the inventor's disclosure or the intervening U.S. patent document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The only inquiry with respect to the claimed invention is whether the prior art disclosure being relied upon anticipates or renders obvious the claimed invention. Applicability of the exception to subject matter in an intervening reference is determined without comparing those disclosures to the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant disclosure in specification under 37 CFR 1.77(b)(6)
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may identify inventor-originated public disclosures in the specification using the format in 37 CFR 1.77(b)(6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification contains a specific reference to an inventor-originated public disclosure made prior to a potential 102(a)(2) disclosure and an oath or declaration under 37 CFR 1.63 is of record, the Office will consider it apparent that the potential 102(a)(2) disclosure is not prior art for that subject matter, provided there is a sufficient explanation of why the exception applies and no contrary evidence. A copy of the prior inventor-originated printed publication must be provided if applicable. Applicants may not use 1.77(b)(6) to add such information after filing; instead use 37 CFR 1.130(b) to submit after filing. Identifying disclosures in the specification may expedite examination and reduce Office actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and limits of AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) (common ownership/obligation to assign)
rubrics_metrics.description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) excepts subject matter disclosed in a U.S. patent document from constituting prior art under 102(a)(2) if the subject matter disclosed and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person not later than the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exception may apply to any U.S. patent document regardless of its potential prior art date (no grace-period limitation). It differs from pre-AIA 103(c) because, if 102(b)(2)(C) is met, the document cannot be applied as prior art under either 102 or 103 (so it cannot be used in anticipation or obviousness rejections). However, the exception does not apply to disclosures that qualify as prior art under 102(a)(1) (disclosures made before the effective filing date). Even if the exception applies, a double patenting rejection (statutory or nonstatutory) may still be made based on the document's claims, and the document may be cited for lack of enablement under 35 U.S.C. 112(a). A document that is excepted by 102(b)(2)(C) cannot serve as a secondary reference in a nonstatutory double patenting rejection because a secondary reference must be prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing common ownership by statement
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear and conspicuous statement by the applicant (or representative) that the claimed invention and the subject matter disclosed in the cited U.S. patent document were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person not later than the effective filing date will be sufficient to establish that the 102(b)(2)(C) exception applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may present supporting evidence such as assignment documents, but are not required to do so. The Office will not request corroborating evidence absent independent evidence raising doubt as to the statement's veracity. A statement is required regardless of any assignment information recorded in the Office's assignment database. The Office treats such statements analogously to statements under pre-AIA 103(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.130 mechanism overview
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR 1.130 provides a mechanism for filing affidavits or declarations to disqualify a disclosure as prior art under AIA 102(a) by relying on exceptions in 102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 CFR 1.130(a) permits affidavits/declarations of attribution (showing disclosure was by inventor/joint inventor or obtained from them). 37 CFR 1.130(b) permits affidavits/declarations of prior public disclosure (showing subject matter was publicly disclosed by the inventor/joint inventor or by someone who obtained it from them before the intervening disclosure or its effective filing date).

rubrics_metrics.name: Content requirements for 37 CFR 1.130(a) (attribution) affidavits/declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.130(a) must establish that the challenged disclosure was made by the inventor or a joint inventor, or that the subject matter disclosed was obtained directly or indirectly from the inventor or joint inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A declaration that is a naked assertion of inventorship without context, explanation, or supporting evidence is insufficient (see EmeraChem Holdings). Where the prior-art authorship includes the inventor or joint inventor named in the application, an unequivocal statement that the inventor(s) invented the subject matter, accompanied by a reasonable explanation for additional authors, may be acceptable absent contrary evidence. Examples illustrate when such declarations withdraw rejections (e.g., where the declaration identifies the inventor and explains coauthors' roles) and when they fail (e.g., failing to explain a coauthor's role or failing to assert inventorship).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on availability of 37 CFR 1.130(a)/(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: The provisions of 37 CFR 1.130 are not available in all circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits/declarations under 1.130 are not available if the rejection is based upon a disclosure made more than one year before the effective filing date of the claimed invention. 1.130 may not be available if the rejection is based on a U.S. patent or published application naming another inventor that claims the same or substantially the same invention and the affidavit/declaration contends derivation by that named inventor; in such cases the applicant may need to file a petition for a derivation proceeding under § 42.401 et seq.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content requirements for 37 CFR 1.130(b) (prior public disclosure) affidavits/declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.130(b) must identify the subject matter publicly disclosed and establish the date and content of the earlier public disclosure by the inventor or joint inventor (or by someone who obtained the subject matter from them).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the earlier public disclosure was a printed publication, the affidavit/declaration must include a copy of the printed publication (1.130(b)(1)). If the earlier disclosure was not a printed publication, the affidavit/declaration must describe the subject matter with sufficient detail and particularity to determine what was publicly disclosed (1.130(b)(2)). The manner of disclosure is not critical — different forms (slides vs journal) or different words do not preclude use of 1.130(b). Examples show that supplying presentation slides can satisfy the printed-publication requirement and withdraw an anticipation rejection when properly supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner practice on making 102(a)(1) and 102(a)(2) rejections (compact prosecution)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a U.S. patent document has a public availability date within the one-year grace period, examiners should consider making both 102(a)(1) and 102(a)(2) rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the examiner cannot foresee how an applicant will respond (e.g., by invoking a 1.130 declaration), making both rejections can avoid additional non-final actions. If an applicant later establishes an exception (e.g., under 102(b)(1)(A) or via 1.130), the examiner may withdraw the appropriate rejection(s). Examples illustrate making both rejections when a reference's publication/issue date is within the grace period; if the 102(a)(1) date were prior to the grace period, a 102(a)(2) rejection would be unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing inventor status when relying on 1.130
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit/declaration under 1.130 may not be sufficient to overcome a 102(a)(2) rejection unless the record also establishes that the affiant is an inventor of the claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a 1.130(a) declaration shows an inventor told the intervening discloser about X but does not state that the declarant invented X, the examiner should maintain the 102(a)(2) rejection because inventorship is not established (Example 3). The applicant can establish inventorship by submitting a new 1.130(a) declaration that states the declarant invented X or by filing an inventor's oath or declaration under 37 CFR 1.63 signed by the inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus-species nuance for prior-public-disclosure exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The equivalence between prior inventor disclosure and later intervening disclosures depends on whether the subject matter is the same in the sense of species vs genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If inventor publicly disclosed a species and an intervening document later discloses a genus that includes that species, the inventor's earlier disclosure is considered the same subject matter and the exception may apply to the genus disclosure. If inventor disclosed a genus and the intervening document discloses a species within that genus, the species in the intervening document remains prior art. If the intervening document discloses an alternative species not previously disclosed by the inventor, that alternative species remains prior art. Examples 1 and 2 under §2155.02 illustrate these outcomes and show that even if an anticipation rejection is withdrawn, an obviousness rejection based on other disclosed species may be appropriate and could be maintained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of 102(b) exceptions on double patenting and enablement rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when a U.S. patent document is not available as prior art under 102 or 103 because a 102(b) exception applies, that document may still be relevant for other rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A document excepted by 102(b)(2)(C) may still be the basis for a statutory or nonstatutory double patenting rejection (its claims can support double patenting), and it may be cited to show the state of the art for a lack of enablement rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a). However, a secondary reference used in a nonstatutory double patenting rejection must itself be prior art; thus, if the 102(b) exception applies, the document cannot be used as that secondary reference.
